title: Permutations and cycles
objectives: Write a permutation in cycle notation and find its order.

screens.title: Follow the arrows
screens.prose: A **permutation** of $\{1, \dots, 8\}$ is a bijection $\sigma$. In two-line notation the bottom row lists $\sigma(1), \dots, \sigma(8)$: here $5, 3, 8, 1, 4, 7, 6, 2$. The arrow diagram draws $k \to \sigma(k)$.
screens.question: Tap the nodes of the loop through 1, in the order the arrows visit them, starting at 1.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Start at 1 and follow its arrow each time.

byKey.order: Those are the right nodes in the wrong order. Follow the arrows from 1.

explain.text: The loop is $1 \to 5 \to 4 \to 1$, the cycle $(1\,5\,4)$. The other loops are $2 \to 3 \to 8 \to 2$ and $6 \to 7 \to 6$.

screens.title: Cycle notation
screens.prose: A **cycle** $(a_1\,a_2 \dots a_k)$ sends each entry to the next and the last back to the first. Cycles with no common entry are **disjoint**. We start each cycle at its smallest entry and leave fixed points out.
screens.question: Which is $\sigma$ in cycle notation?

options.why: You stopped after two loops. 6 and 7 swap, which is the cycle $(6\,7)$.
You followed the arrows backwards. That is $\sigma^{-1}$.

hints.text: Each loop of the diagram is a cycle.

feedback.correct: Right. The permutations of $n$ items form $S_n$, with $|S_n| = n!$ (`counting` l2).
feedback.generic: Not quite. Write one cycle per loop, in the arrows' direction.

explain.text: Three loops give three disjoint cycles: $(1\,5\,4)(2\,3\,8)(6\,7)$. $S_8$ holds $8! = 40320$ permutations in all.

screens.title: Composing cycles
screens.prose: Composition reads right to left, as in l1: $\alpha\beta$ means do $\beta$, then $\alpha$. Work out the bottom rows of $(1\,2)(2\,3)$ and of $(2\,3)(1\,2)$.
screens.question: Fill in where each product sends 1, 2 and 3.

hints.text: For $(1\,2)(2\,3)$: 1 is fixed by $(2\,3)$, then $(1\,2)$ sends it to 2.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Do the right-hand cycle first.

byKey.r0c1: Under $(2\,3)$, 1 stays put; then $(1\,2)$ sends 1 to 2.
byKey.r1c1: Under $(1\,2)$, 1 goes to 2; then $(2\,3)$ sends 2 to 3.

explain.text: Right to left, $(1\,2)(2\,3)$ sends $1 \to 2$, $2 \to 3$, $3 \to 1$: the cycle $(1\,2\,3)$. The other order gives $(1\,3\,2)$, so these cycles do not commute.

screens.title: Disjoint cycles
screens.prose: $(1\,2)$ and $(2\,3)$ share the entry 2, and they did not commute. Now take $(1\,2)$ and $(3\,4)$.
screens.question: Is $(1\,2)(3\,4) = (3\,4)(1\,2)$?

options.text: Yes: they move different entries, so the order does not matter.

options.why: You generalised from $(1\,2)(2\,3)$. Those share an entry; disjoint cycles act on separate entries.

options.text: Only when both cycles have the same length.
options.why: Length is not the reason. $(1\,2)$ and $(3\,4\,5)$ commute too.

hints.text: Track each entry through both orders.
Each entry is moved by at most one of the cycles.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Follow 1 and 3 through each order.

explain.text: Each entry is moved by at most one of the two cycles. So the order of doing them cannot matter, and disjoint cycles may be listed in any order.

screens.title: The order of a permutation
screens.prose: The order of $\sigma$ is the least $k \ge 1$ with $\sigma^k = e$. For disjoint cycles there is a rule.
screens.question: Order the proof. Leave out the false line.

lines.text: Disjoint cycles move different points, so $\sigma^k$ acts on each cycle separately.
On a cycle of length $\ell$, $\sigma^k$ fixes its points exactly when $\ell \mid k$ (l4).
So $\sigma^k = e$ exactly when every cycle length divides $k$.
The least such k is the lcm of the cycle lengths.
So the order is the product of the cycle lengths.
lines.why: You multiplied the lengths. $(1\,2\,3\,4)(5\,6)$ has order 4, not 8: 4 is already a multiple of 2.

hints.text: Treat each cycle on its own.
An $\ell$-cycle has order $\ell$, so its powers give $e$ at multiples of $\ell$.
Separate, divide, every length, least common multiple.

feedback.correct: That is the proof: the order is the lcm of the lengths.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Split into cycles first.

byKey.left-out: You left out a step the proof needs.

explain.text: Each cycle returns home at multiples of its length. All return together first at the lcm. So $\operatorname{ord}(\sigma) = \operatorname{lcm}$ of the cycle lengths.

hints.text: $\sigma^6 = e$, and no smaller power is.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Find the least common multiple of the lengths.

byKey.prod: You multiplied, $3 \times 3 \times 2 = 18$. The two 3-cycles return together every 3 steps.
byKey.max: You took the longest cycle. The 2-cycle is not home after 3 steps.

explain.text: $\operatorname{lcm}(3, 3, 2) = 6$. After 6 steps each 3-cycle has gone round twice and the swap three times.

screens.title: More orders
screens.prose: Use the lcm rule on two more permutations in $S_8$.
screens.question: Fill in each order.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Take the lcm of the cycle lengths.

explain.text: $\operatorname{lcm}(2, 3) = 6$ and $\operatorname{lcm}(3, 5) = 15$. Here the lengths are coprime, so the lcm is the product.

screens.title: The largest order
screens.prose: In $S_7$ a permutation splits the 7 entries into cycles whose lengths add to at most 7. Its order is the lcm of the lengths.
screens.question: What is the largest order of an element of $S_7$?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Compare the lcms of the ways to split 7.

byKey.seven: You took one long cycle. A 3-cycle with a 4-cycle does better.

explain.text: The best split is $3 + 4$, with $\operatorname{lcm} = 12$. In $S_8$ the best is $3 + 5$, giving 15.

screens.title: Product or lcm?
screens.prose: For $(1\,2)(3\,4\,5)$ the product of the lengths, 6, was the order. Now take $\tau = (1\,2\,3\,4)(5\,6)$.
screens.question: What is the order of $\tau$?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Use the lcm, not the product.

byKey.prod: You multiplied the lengths. After 4 steps the swap $(5\,6)$ has gone round twice, so $\tau^4 = e$.
byKey.sum: You added the lengths. The order is the lcm.

explain.text: $\tau^4$ sends the 4-cycle round once and the swap twice, so $\tau^4 = e$. The product 8 agrees with the lcm only when the lengths are coprime.

screens.title: A perfect shuffle of 8
screens.prose: A perfect **out-shuffle** cuts the deck in half and interleaves the halves, top card staying on top. Number the 8 positions 0 to 7. The card at position $k$ moves to $2k \bmod 7$ for $k < 7$, and card 7 stays.
screens.question: How many out-shuffles return 8 cards to their starting order?

hints.text: So three shuffles restore the deck.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Find the order of 2 modulo 7.

byKey.eight: You used the number of cards. The shuffle's order is ord(2) mod 7.
byKey.seven: You used the modulus 7. Find the power of 2 that is 1 modulo 7.

explain.text: Position $k$ goes to $2k \bmod 7$, so after $m$ shuffles to $2^m k$. That is $k$ again when $2^m \equiv 1$, first at $m = 3$. As a permutation the shuffle is $(1\,2\,4)(3\,6\,5)$.

screens.title: A full deck
screens.prose: For 52 cards the out-shuffle sends position $k$ to $2k \bmod 51$ for $k < 51$, and the bottom card stays. A dealer claims 7 perfect out-shuffles randomise a deck.
screens.question: How many perfect out-shuffles return a 52-card deck to its starting order?

feedback.correct: Right: 8. Seven perfect shuffles leave a fixed order, and the eighth restores it.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Find the order of 2 modulo 51.

byKey.deck: That is the in-shuffle's order. The out-shuffle keeps the top card, giving 8.

explain.text: $2^8 = 256 \equiv 1 \pmod{51}$ and no smaller power is 1, so 8 out-shuffles restore the deck. Perfect shuffles are a permutation of order 8, not randomness.

screens.title: Cycles by machine
screens.prose: Write `cycles(perm)` for a 0-based one-line tuple. Return the cycles of length 2 or more, each from its smallest entry, sorted by it. Then `perm_order` is the lcm of their lengths. $\sigma$ is `(4, 2, 7, 0, 3, 6, 5, 1)` 0-based. Passing these cases settles these permutations only.
screens.question: Write cycles, and fix perm_order to use the lcm.

tests.name: out52
tests.setup: out = tuple(2 * k % 51 if k < 51 else 51 for k in range(52))

tests.name: in52
tests.setup: ins = tuple((2 * k + 1) % 53 for k in range(52))

widget.how: The first Check starts Python, which takes a few seconds. Submit runs 8 hidden tests; each must equal the expected value exactly.

hints.text: Walk from each unvisited start until you return, recording the entries.
Starting at each index in increasing order makes each cycle begin at its smallest entry.

feedback.correct: All eight pass, including the 52-card shuffles of orders 8 and 52.
feedback.generic: Not yet. Read the first failing row.

explain.text: The out-shuffle of 52 has order 8 and the in-shuffle, $k \mapsto 2k + 1 \bmod 53$, has order 52. The product rule fails $\tau = (1\,2\,3\,4)(5\,6)$, order 4.

ideas: Every permutation is a product of disjoint cycles: $\sigma = (1\,5\,4)(2\,3\,8)(6\,7)$.
Products read right to left, and overlapping cycles need not commute: $(1\,2)(2\,3) = (1\,2\,3)$.
The order is the lcm of the cycle lengths, so 8 out-shuffles restore 52 cards.

formula.name: Order of a permutation
formula.note: The lengths of the disjoint cycles.

summary.trap: The order is not the product of the lengths: $(1\,2\,3\,4)(5\,6)$ has order 4, not 8.

quiz.question: How is the identity of $S_5$ written in cycle notation, with fixed points left out?

options.text: With no cycles at all, written $e$

options.why: You wrote a 5-cycle. That moves every entry; the identity moves none.
You kept the fixed points. Our convention leaves them out, so nothing is left.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Which entries does the identity move?

explain.text: The identity fixes every entry, and fixed points are left out, so it has no cycles. We write it $e$.

quiz.question: Number the square's corners as in l1. Which permutation of the corners is the flip $s$?

options.why: That is the quarter turn $r$, which moves each corner to the next.
That flip fixes corners 1 and 3: it is $r^3s$, the flip in $y = x$.

feedback.correct: Right. So $D_4$ sits inside $S_4$ as 8 of its 24 elements.
feedback.generic: Not quite. The vertical-axis flip swaps left and right.

explain.text: The flip in the vertical axis swaps corners 1 and 2, and 3 and 4: $s = (1\,2)(3\,4)$. With $r = (1\,2\,3\,4)$ these generate a copy of $D_4$ in $S_4$.

quiz.question: What is $(1\,3)(1\,2)$ as a single cycle?

options.why: You applied the left-hand cycle first. Right to left: 1 goes to 2 first.
You treated the cycles as disjoint. They share 1, so multiply them out.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Multiply right to left, entry by entry.

explain.text: $(1\,2)$ first: $1 \to 2$, then $(1\,3)$ leaves 2. And $2 \to 1 \to 3$, $3 \to 3 \to 1$. So the product is $(1\,2\,3)$.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Count the orders of 5 items.

byKey.five: You counted the items. Count the orders of 5 items instead.

explain.text: There are $5 \times 4 \times 3 \times 2 \times 1 = 120$ orders of 5 items (`counting` l2), so $|S_5| = 120$.
